$comment: Every number this page draws, tied to the committed blob it came from.
The page's thesis is 'every number is traceable to the repository it came
from'. Until this file existed that was a slogan: the plates and the prose
were checked against EACH OTHER (gate.mjs check 9) and against nothing else,
so two authored strings could agree perfectly and both be false. Three rounds
of audits found exactly that.
A row is a derivation, not a citation. `extractor` is a shell command run
against $BLOB — the file fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at `ref`,
which is a COMMIT SHA, never a branch name. Its stdout must equal `value`
exactly. Nobody has to trust the number; they run the command.
`drawn_on` is where the value appears on this page. build/claims.mjs checks
both directions: every row must re-derive, AND every number a plate draws
must have a row here or an entry in `exempt`. A claims file that only
verified the numbers it happened to list would be the same gate-that-cannot-
fail this project has already shipped twice.

applied-web.note: The in-browser ONNX build is NOT on main. The commit is pushed and public, so it pins and re-derives like any other — but the page must say which branch it is reading, and does.

It is deliberately not cached and will break if the live build changes, which is the point: the README says the live page and the repo diverge here, and this is what keeps that sentence honest.

The number the page was suppressing. The parallel ratio moved 6.89x -> 6.38x between the quick and the rigorous run — an 8% spread, WIDER than the 4% spread on the SIMD ratio that the page already discloses. jetpack's own ENVIRONMENT.md warns about it. Publishing the smaller disagreement and hiding the larger one is the only place this page let the flattering number win, so the README now states it.
The same ratio as jetpack.speedup, at two decimals, so the 6.89 -> 6.38 spread the README now discloses is stated in numbers that both derive.
The dispatch table itself, not the import list — the import list agrees at 36, but routes are what the function actually serves.
This is the row that keeps the hero honest: the artifact itself says the score was produced with the rules layer alone, which is what the plate labels it.

claims.extractor: python3 -c "import ast,sys;t=ast.parse(open(sys.argv[1]).read());print(sum(1 for n in ast.walk(t) if isinstance(n,ast.AnnAssign) and getattr(n.target,'id','')=='PATTERNS' for s in ast.walk(n.value) if isinstance(s,ast.Constant) and isinstance(s.value,str)))" "$BLOB"
claims.note: Parsed, not grepped. A second method — counting r-string lines inside the PATTERNS block — also gives 201.
The build really does fail below this: it is a CI flag, not a doc sentence.
The byte length of the committed artifact, read from the contents API at that SHA. Not on main — see the applied-web repo entry.
The full three-layer cascade's score, which survives in exactly one line of prose because the run that produced it was overwritten. The page says so, and now proves the line still says it.
Pins the citation itself. If the tracker grows a line above 378, this fails and the README's reference is corrected rather than silently pointing at the wrong row.

The plate used to draw '8 FOUND, 8 FIXED'. Eight is true and eight is documented, but it is an AUDIT FINDING, not a property of any file — the previous extractor here reached 8 by counting the word 'IDOR' in comments, which is the page counting its own prose. It happened to be right and would have broken silently on the next comment edit. Seven regression tests IS a file property, and it is the more honest number besides: TaskListService.test.ts contributes 0, which is exactly the gap the README admits. The eighth vulnerability keeps its story in prose, where testimony belongs.

claims.extractor: grep -cE '^ALTER TABLE .* FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' "$BLOB"
claims.note: Anchored to ^ALTER TABLE on purpose. A bare `grep -c 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY'` returns 8, because the file's own header comment explains what FORCE does — the same prose-counting mistake as the row above, in a file where it would have inflated the claim. user_profiles is deliberately excluded from RLS (0002_enable_rls.sql:21-22), so 'every tenant table' is seven, and the README now says seven.

The canonical Adler-32 vector for the input "Wikipedia", asserted for both the scalar and the vectorised path (Adler32Test.java:36-37). It is now drawn as one string per row rather than eight <text> elements, so it appears whole in the plate and needs no per-glyph exemptions. The stronger claim on the plate — bit-identical to java.util.zip — is the separate matchesJdkAcrossSizes test, which compares both paths across 26 input sizes.

$unpinnable_note: This list held exactly one row — AutoML's '2 approval gates' — filed under
the reason 'the repo is private'. That diagnosis was wrong, and the way it
was wrong matters more than the number.
The count was not merely unverifiable. It was FALSE: the reproducible count
of human-gate stages is four (preprocessing await_approval, feature
engineering await_review, training propose_model and await_review). By
filing it as 'private, therefore unpinnable' this file certified a wrong
number as an acceptable one, and printed a friendly note where it should
have failed. A category that excuses a claim from being checked will,
sooner or later, be where a false claim goes to live.
So there is no such category any more. Plate VI no longer draws a count at
all; it draws the mechanism and says on its face that this is the one
section a reader cannot check. Anything drawn must derive or be exempt.

external.why: Vercel's Hobby-tier cap of 12 Serverless Functions per deployment is a platform fact, not a measurement of this repository. The previous extractor grepped `caps deployments at 12` out of api/index.ts — the author's own comment — so the page was citing itself and calling it derivation. What the repo genuinely proves is the consequence: one function serving 36 routes, which cadence.handlers derives.

$comment: Numbers a plate draws that are not measurements of a repository — names,
versions, viewBox geometry, and the glyphs of a hex constant. Each needs a
reason. Prefer a file-scoped key ('plate-2-jetpack.svg:6') over a bare one:
a global exemption for '6' would wave through an unsourced 6 anywhere in
the document. claims.mjs also fails on an exemption no plate uses, so this
list cannot quietly accumulate excuses for numbers that are already gone.
